items.snippet: # US AI megadeals drive global VC to USD $331 billion. Global venture capital in...
items.raw_snippet: # US AI megadeals drive global VC to USD $331 billion. Global venture capital investment rose to USD $330.9 billion in the first quarter of 2026, driven by a cluster of very large AI-related funding rounds, according to KPMG. The Americas attracted USD $270.1 billion in venture capital during the quarter, more than 80 per cent of the global total. Europe recorded USD $25.7 billion, a 14-quarter high, while Asia reached USD $31.8 billion, a 12-quarter high. Software was the largest sector for venture capital investment worldwide, drawing a quarterly record of USD $225.2 billion. Among the biggest were a USD $2 billion round for China-based Rokid and a USD $2 billion round for Singapore-based DayOne. China recorded a particularly strong quarter, supported by renewed interest in AI, deep tech, biotech, semiconductors, and space-related businesses. Europe and Asia remained slow, but the US showed some improvement, with USD $47.8 billion raised during the quarter compared with USD $66.7 billion during all of 2025.

items.title: Corporate Law in Orbit: The SpaceX–xAI Merger and Regulatory Strain – Journal of High Technology Law
items.snippet: # Corporate Law in Orbit: The SpaceX–xAI Merger and Regulatory Strain. When repo...
items.raw_snippet: # Corporate Law in Orbit: The SpaceX–xAI Merger and Regulatory Strain. When reports first surfaced that Elon Musk was considering a merger between SpaceX and his artificial intelligence company, xAI, the idea seemed almost too on-brand to be surprising. This kind of triangular merger is a well-known structure in corporate law. Unlike a straightforward merger between competitors, the SpaceX–xAI deal combines companies operating in different, but increasingly interconnected markets. Adding a powerful AI company into that ecosystem raises questions about whether the combined entity could leverage control over infrastructure, data, and computation in ways that disadvantage competitors. The deal does not obviously violate corporate law principles, antitrust rules, or regulatory requirements. The SpaceX–xAI merger offers a glimpse of what that future looks like: legally permissible, carefully structured, and deeply challenging for regulators and courts tasked with overseeing technologies that evolve faster than the rules designed to govern them.

items.title: The Federal Government Is Buying AI at Scale — and Flying Blind on Records Management
items.snippet: *GAO-26-107859, “Artificial Intelligence Acquisitions: Agencies Should Collect a...
items.raw_snippet: *GAO-26-107859, “Artificial Intelligence Acquisitions: Agencies Should Collect and Apply Lessons Learned to Improve Future Procurements” (April 2026)*. The GAO examined 13 AI acquisitions across four agencies, analyzing 44 contracts and agreements awarded between September 2018 and February 2025. The acquisitions span a striking range of capability and consequence: machine learning systems that assess veterans’ disability claims; computer vision systems that perform facial comparison at airport security checkpoints; natural language processing tools that scan veterans’ survey responses for indicators of suicidal ideation; deep learning models that detect seizures; generative AI platforms that help write federal hazard mitigation plans. Across this range, the GAO identified six recurring challenge areas: access to subject matter experts; protections for government data and intellectual property rights; traditional acquisition timeframes and contract approaches; requirements definition and contract terms; early testing and continuous evaluation; and AI pricing and overall cost. The knowledge sharing gap, which forms the report’s core finding, is straightforward: none of the four agencies in scope had policies requiring officials to systematically document lessons learned from AI acquisitions.

items.title: Stop Reinventing AI Policy. Start Funding What Already Works. - Chronicle of Philanthropy
items.snippet: The central challenge in AI policy today is not how to invent new principles but...
items.raw_snippet: The central challenge in AI policy today is not how to invent new principles but how to ensure that the hard-won progress of recent years is implemented, enforced, and sustained. Overseas, the European AI and Society Fund ensures the public has a voice in regulating the industry, and in Australia, the Minderoo Foundation supports a network of academics and policy institutions working on issues such as corporate governance of AI. That means resisting the temptation to chase every new AI headline and instead focusing on the quieter work of funding cross-border collaboration, policy training and research centers, and organizations that translate international norms into national practice. With sustained support, the AI policy field can advance on its gains and demonstrate that democratic oversight of advanced technology is both possible and effective. It is a field in need of reinforcement — through multi-year commitments, support for enforcement capacity, and sustained investment in the institutions now responsible for democratic oversight of AI.

items.raw_snippet: # AI as a Service (AIaaS) - The Future of Integrating Artificial Intelligence. ai as a service (aiaas) - the future of integrating artificial intelligence. Therefore, many organizations are choosing to partner with reputable third-party providers offering artificial intelligence solutions, or AI as a service (AIaaS). Businesses may consider AIaaS as part of their AI/ML development services to gain access to valuable frameworks and models, which are deployed on the service provider's cloud servers, freeing up computing resources for the organization. By collaborating with reliable firms providing AI product development services, businesses can select customized AIaaS packages and embark on their digital transformation journeys at a comfortable pace. These service providers utilize AI and ML tools for advanced analytics, sharing reports with organizations that adopt intelligence-as-a-service solutions, thereby saving them the costs and resources associated with deploying AI data analytical models on-premise. items.raw_snippet: (To quote just one indelible line, from 2015, “I think A.I. will probably most likely lead to the end of the world, but in the meantime there’ll be great companies created with serious machine learning.”) Even in his recent blog post, Altman wrote that “the fear and anxiety about AI is justified; we are in the process of witnessing the largest change to society in a long time, and perhaps ever.” Who, exactly, does he think is to blame for stoking hysteria? In his blog post, Altman wrote, without apparent irony, that the prospect of controlling artificial general intelligence was like the “ring of power” from “The Lord of the Rings”: it “makes people do crazy things.” OpenAI’s main rival, Anthropic, has marketed itself as the industry’s safety-minded good guys.
